title: Article 19 — Six freedoms and reasonable restrictions

content.overview: Article 19(1) guarantees six freedoms to citizens: speech and expression; assembly peaceably and without arms; association; movement throughout India; residence in any part of India; and practice of any profession, or carrying on any occupation, trade or business. The right to property in former clause (f) was omitted. Clauses (2) to (6) allow reasonable restrictions only on the grounds written in the matching clause. A restriction that is not on a listed ground, or that is not reasonable, is outside the clause. Reasonableness is case-law and is not given a test here.
content.study: Confirm the claimant is a citizen. Match the freedom to its restriction clause. Do not import public-order grounds into speech unless clause (2) lists them, and do not use clause (2) grounds for a trade restriction.

sections.heading: Speech and expression
sections.body: Restrictions must fall within Article 19(2) grounds. Vague bans attract close scrutiny.

learningObjectives: Pair each freedom with its restriction clause.
Keep reasonableness on the case-law gate.
enhancement.definition: Article 19 guarantees six specified freedoms to citizens, subject only to reasonable restrictions on the grounds in clauses (2) to (6).
enhancement.legalPrinciple: The restriction must fit the clause enacted for that freedom. An unlisted ground is not saved by calling it reasonable.
enhancement.statutoryFramework: Constitution of India, Article 19. Former clause (1)(f) omitted by the Forty-fourth Amendment.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Clause (2) restricts speech on the sovereignty and integrity of India, security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, decency or morality, contempt of court, defamation, or incitement to an offence. Clause (3) restricts assembly on the sovereignty and integrity of India and public order. Clause (4) restricts association on those grounds as well. Clause (5) restricts movement and residence on the interests of the general public or the protection of the interests of a Scheduled Tribe. Clause (6) restricts profession, occupation, trade or business on the interests of the general public, and it also allows a law prescribing professional or technical qualifications, and a State monopoly. Speech grounds cannot be copied into trade. A non-citizen does not plead Article 19; Article 14 or 21 may still be open.
examples: A speaking ban is defended only as a trade regulation. Clause (2), not clause (6), is the speech clause.
A non-citizen journalist pleads Article 19. Citizenship is missing.
A State creates a monopoly in a trade. Clause (6) is the provision to read, not clause (2).
enhancement.problemApplication: Identify the freedom, the clause number, and whether the stated ground is written in that clause. Then flag reasonableness for authority.
distinctions: Article 19 citizens vs Article 14 any person
Clause (2) speech grounds vs clause (6) trade grounds
Six present freedoms vs omitted property freedom
Reasonable restriction vs an unlisted ground
